summary.en: Use prototypes to describe calls before their definitions and keep declarations consistent.
summary.bn: প্রোটোটাইপ আগে লিখে দিলে পরে সংজ্ঞা থাকা ফাংশনও ঠিকভাবে ডাকা যায়।

notes: C99 removed implicit function declarations; C23 makes an empty parameter list mean no parameters.

examples.title: Prototype above main, definition below
examples.explanationHtml: The prototype lets main call triple before its body appears. The definition agrees on one int parameter and an int result.

examples.title: Parameter names may differ
examples.explanationHtml: The declaration omits names. The definition adds left and right, while the types and parameter order remain unchanged.

examples.title: A no-argument prototype
examples.explanationHtml: void inside the parentheses tells C17 that the caller supplies no arguments. The return type void separately says there is no result value.

examples.title: Mutually visible helper declarations
examples.explanationHtml: Both signatures are visible before main. total can call fee even though fee is defined last.

quiz.prompt: Which part distinguishes a function definition from a prototype?
quiz.explanation: Both describe a type, but only a definition supplies the statements that execute.

quiz.prompt: Why must a declaration precede a C17 function call?
options: The compiler needs the function type to check the call
It allocates every local variable in advance
quiz.explanation: A visible type supports argument and result checking. A prototype does not execute or force inlining.

quiz.prompt: With twice declared before main and defined afterward, which result is printed?
quiz.explanation: The unnamed prototype parameter and named definition parameter describe the same int input.

quiz.prompt: Which prototype explicitly accepts no arguments in C17?
quiz.explanation: void in the parameter list means no parameters. Empty parentheses in C17 omit parameter-type information.

quiz.prompt: What does a header normally share for a helper defined in another source file?
options: A second externally linked body in every file
quiz.explanation: Sharing one declaration keeps callers and the implementation consistent without multiplying definitions.

quiz.prompt: Which value does a helper with two declared int parameters return here?
quiz.explanation: Different parameter names do not reverse positions. Nine minus four is five.

quiz.prompt: When did C remove implicit function declarations?
quiz.explanation: C99 requires modern code to declare functions before use instead of relying on old implicit assumptions.

quiz.prompt: Can prototype parameter names differ from names in the matching definition?
options: Yes, compatible types and order are what matter
quiz.explanation: Names in a prototype document the interface. Positional parameter types define call compatibility.

quiz.prompt: A declared no-argument helper is called twice. How many unit labels appear?
quiz.explanation: The prototype prints nothing. Each of the two calls prints one label.

quiz.prompt: A call compiles with a prototype, but its body is never linked. Where can failure occur?
options: It must run and return zero
quiz.explanation: A prototype supplies type information, not the implementation needed by the linker.

A declaration must be visible before its function is called.

examQuestions.question: Distinguish a prototype from a definition and explain why a shared header is useful.
examQuestions.answerHtml: A prototype supplies the return and parameter types but no body. A definition supplies a compatible body. A shared header gives callers and the implementation the same declaration. The implementation still needs one linked definition.

#include <stdio.h>

int twice(int);

int twice(int number)
{
    return number * 2;
}

int main(void)
{
    printf("%d\n", twice(7));
    return 0;
}

14

The unnamed prototype parameter and named definition parameter describe the same int input.

examQuestions.question: Read one integer from 0 to 100; add twice the value to twice its successor. Put a prototype above main and the definition below. Print Value: before input, then the integer result.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
#include <stdio.h>
int twice(int hours);
int main(void)
{
    int value;
    puts("Value:");
    if (scanf("%d", &value) != 1 || value < 0 || value > 100) {
        return 1;
    }
    printf("%d\n", twice(value) + twice(value + 1));
    return 0;
}
int twice(int hours)
{
    return hours * 2;
}

Match the return and parameter types in both declarations.

For input 0, the program prints:

Value:
2
